title: Ethical Hacking and Capture the Flag
summary: Think like an attacker to defend like a pro: the law and ethics of hacking, how Capture the Flag competitions work, decoding hidden messages, finding secrets in files and web pages, and how ethical hackers report problems and build careers.
learn: The difference between ethical and criminal hacking, and the Computer Misuse Act
How Capture the Flag competitions work
How to recognise and decode binary, hex, Base64 and ROT13
How data can be hidden in files and images
How to investigate a web page using its source code
Responsible disclosure, bug bounties and cyber security careers
intro: Ethical hackers are paid to break into systems, with permission, so the weaknesses can be fixed before criminals find them. In this topic you'll learn the rules that keep hacking legal, then sharpen your skills in Capture the Flag (CTF) challenges: decoding messages, uncovering hidden data and investigating web pages, all on practice systems built for the job.

pages.title: Hackers with permission
pages.spec: Explain the difference between ethical and criminal hacking and the rules of the Computer Misuse Act
pages.summary: Ethical hackers test systems only with clear permission and within agreed limits, then report what they find so it can be fixed. Accessing any system without permission is a crime under the Computer Misuse Act 1990, even "just to look".
pages.starter: A friend shows you how to log in to another pupil's account "just to prove it's possible". Is that hacking? Is it a crime?
sc: I can describe white, black and grey hat hackers
I can explain the three main offences in the Computer Misuse Act
I can explain why permission and scope matter

b: White hat: ethical hackers who test with permission to make systems safer
Black hat: criminals who break in to steal, damage or show off
Grey hat: break in without permission, then tell the owner, which is still illegal
Only one of these is a career
Applies across the UK, including Northern Ireland
Offence 1: unauthorised access to computer material (e.g. using someone's password)
Offence 2: unauthorised access with intent to commit further crimes
Offence 3: unauthorised acts to impair a computer (e.g. spreading malware)
Penalties range from fines to life imprisonment for the most serious cases
slides.n: Starter answer: yes, it is unauthorised access, an offence under section 1 even if nothing is changed. Schools treat it very seriously.

b: Ethical hackers get written permission before testing
The scope says exactly which systems and methods are allowed
Stay inside the scope; report everything; damage nothing
In this topic we only ever hack practice systems made for it

blocks.text: What is ethical hacking?

**[[ethical hacking]]** means testing computer systems for weaknesses **with the owner's permission**, so the problems can be fixed before criminals find them. Companies pay for **[[penetration testing]]** (pen testing): a planned, authorised attack on their own systems.

blocks.caption: The three "hats"
head: Type
Permission?
Why they hack
Legal?
rows: To steal, damage, spy or show off
Curiosity, then they tell the owner

blocks.text: The Computer Misuse Act 1990
The **[[Computer Misuse Act]]** is the main UK law against hacking, and it applies in Northern Ireland. Its main offences are:

items: **Unauthorised access** to computer material: for example logging in to someone else's account, even just to look.
**Unauthorised access with intent to commit further offences**: for example breaking in to steal money or data.
**Unauthorised acts that impair a computer**: for example spreading malware or crashing a website.

blocks.text: "I was only looking" or "I didn't change anything" is not a defence. Accessing any account or system without permission is a crime, and schools treat it very seriously.
Permission and scope

Before an ethical hacker starts, they agree a written **[[scope]]**: exactly which systems they may test, which methods are allowed, and when. Anything outside the scope is off-limits, even if it looks interesting. Throughout this topic, you'll only practise on systems built for training, like CTF challenge websites.

blocks.title: Legal or not?
steps: Read the eight scenario cards (e.g. "A pupil guesses a teacher's password to change a mark").
Decide for each: legal ethical hacking, or a Computer Misuse Act offence? If it's an offence, which one?
For each illegal scenario, write what the person should have done instead.

q.q: Choose two illegal scenarios: which offence, and what should the person have done?
q.a: E.g. "Guessing a teacher's password to change a mark: offence 2 (unauthorised access to commit a further offence). They should never do it; if they found a weakness by accident, they should tell IT straight away." "Logging in to a friend's account to read messages: offence 1, unauthorised access. Ask permission or don't do it."

q.q: Explain why a grey hat hacker can still be breaking the law.
q.a: They access systems without permission, which is unauthorised access under the Computer Misuse Act, even if they mean well and report it afterwards.

check.q: What makes hacking "ethical"?
o: The owner has given permission and it's done within agreed limits

check.q: Which law makes unauthorised access to computers illegal in the UK?
Logging in to a friend's account without permission "just to look" is...
o: an offence under the Computer Misuse Act

check.q: What is the scope of a penetration test?
o: The agreed list of systems and methods allowed

practice.q: Describe the three main offences in the Computer Misuse Act.
practice.a: Unauthorised access to computer material (1); unauthorised access with intent to commit further offences (1); unauthorised acts to impair a computer/e.g. spreading malware (1).

practice.q: Explain the difference between a white hat and a black hat hacker.
practice.a: White hat has permission and aims to find/fix weaknesses (1); black hat has no permission and aims to steal/damage/cause harm (1).

pages.title: Inside a Capture the Flag
pages.spec: Describe how CTF competitions work and use a structured approach to solve challenges
pages.summary: Capture the Flag competitions are legal hacking games. In a "jeopardy" CTF, teams solve puzzles in categories such as cryptography, forensics and web to find hidden text strings called flags and score points.
pages.starter: You find a note that says "The answer is hidden in plain sight." What would you do first?
sc: I can describe jeopardy and attack-defence CTFs
I can name common CTF challenge categories
I can use a structured method to solve a challenge

b: A legal competition where you hack systems built for the game
Find a "flag": a secret string like FLAG{h1dd3n_1n_pla1n_s1ght}
Submit flags to score points
Played by pupils, students and professionals worldwide

b: Jeopardy CTF: a board of challenges, more points for harder ones
Attack-defence CTF: defend your own server while attacking others' (advanced)
Categories: cryptography, forensics, web, OSINT, reverse engineering, puzzles
Teams split up challenges by their strengths

Look at everything: files, text, source code, file names

blocks.text: Capture the Flag

A **[[Capture the Flag]]** (CTF) competition is a legal hacking game. Organisers build challenges on purpose, hiding a **[[flag]]**, usually a string such as FLAG{y0u_f0und_m3}, inside each one. Finding and submitting the flag scores points. CTFs are run for schools (such as the NCSC's CyberFirst competitions), universities and professional security teams.

blocks.caption: Common challenge categories
head: Category
What you do
Example
rows: A flag hidden inside an image's data
A flag in a page's HTML comments
Open-source intelligence: find information that's publicly available
Work out where a (fictional) photo was taken
Work out what a program does
Find the password a small program expects

blocks.text: How to approach a challenge

blocks.title: The CTF method
items: Read: titles and descriptions usually contain hints
Look: open everything, including file names, source code and metadata
Recognise: what does this look like? Binary? Base64? A hash?
Try: use tools such as CyberChef, and keep notes of what you tried
Reflect: if stuck, re-read the challenge or take a hint

blocks.text: **[[CyberChef]]** is a free browser tool made by GCHQ, often called "the cyber Swiss Army knife". It can convert between encodings, decrypt simple ciphers and analyse data, all without installing anything.

blocks.title: First flags
steps: Log in to the practice CTF your teacher has set up.
Choose roles: a reader (reads challenges and hints), a solver (tries ideas) and a note-taker.
Solve as many starter challenges as you can in 25 minutes. Rotate roles after each flag.
Record each flag and the method you used.

q.q: Write down one flag you found and explain step by step how you found it.
q.a: Depends on the challenge, e.g. "Challenge 'Look closer': I opened the page source, found an HTML comment containing FLAG{s0urc3_c0d3}, and submitted it."

q.q: What did your team do when you got stuck?
q.a: E.g. re-read the description for clues, tried a different tool in CyberChef, swapped roles, or used a hint.

check.q: What is a flag in a CTF?
o: A secret string you find and submit to score points
check.why: Flags prove you solved a challenge.

check.q: In a jeopardy CTF...
o: teams choose challenges from a board of categories

check.q: What does OSINT stand for?
Who made CyberChef?

practice.q: Describe what a Capture the Flag competition is.
practice.a: A legal hacking competition on systems built for the purpose (1); teams find hidden "flags" to score points (1).

practice.q: Name three common CTF challenge categories and say what each involves.
practice.a: Any three with descriptions: cryptography/decoding (1); forensics/hidden data in files (1); web/investigating websites (1); OSINT/finding public information (1); reverse engineering/working out how a program works (1).

pages.title: Codes and encodings
pages.spec: Recognise and decode binary, hexadecimal, Base64 and ROT13, and explain the difference between encoding and encryption
pages.summary: Encodings change data into a different format so it can be stored or sent, but anyone can reverse them. Spotting binary, hex, Base64 and ROT13 by their look is a key CTF skill. Unlike encryption, encoding has no secret key.
pages.starter: What do these have in common? 01001000 01101001 / 48 69 / SGk= / Uv. (Hint: they all say the same thing.)
sc: I can recognise binary, hex, Base64 and ROT13
I can decode them using CyberChef
I can explain the difference between encoding and encryption

b: Encoding: changing data's format so it can be stored or sent (no secret key)
Anyone who knows the encoding can reverse it
Encryption: scrambling data with a secret key so only key-holders can read it
CTFs often hide flags in layers of encoding
slides.n: Starter: they all say "Hi" in binary, hex, Base64 and ROT13.

b: Binary: only 0s and 1s, often in groups of 8
Hex: digits 0-9 and letters A-F, often in pairs
Base64: upper and lower case letters, digits, + and /, often ending in = or ==
ROT13: looks like normal words, but scrambled; shift letters by 13
Paste the text into the Input box
Drag in a recipe: "From Base64", "From Hex", "ROT13"
Try "Magic": it guesses the encoding for you
Layered? Stack several steps in one recipe

blocks.text: Encoding versus encryption

**[[encoding]]** changes data into a different format so it can be stored or transmitted, such as turning a picture into text so it can travel in an email. There's **no secret key**: anyone who recognises the encoding can reverse it. **Encryption** uses a secret key, so only the right people can read the data.
Encoding is NOT security. Developers sometimes "hide" passwords using Base64, thinking they're protected. Anyone can decode them in seconds.
Recognising encodings

blocks.caption: Spot the encoding
head: Encoding
What it looks like
"Hi" in this format
rows: Only 0 and 1, often in groups of 8
Letters, digits, + and /, often ending in =

blocks.text: ROT13 is a Caesar cipher with a shift of 13. Because the alphabet has 26 letters, doing ROT13 twice gets you back to the start, so the same operation encodes and decodes.

blocks.title: Peeling the layers
blocks.context: A CTF challenge gives you: RkxBR3tyb3QxM19pc19uMHRfc2VjdXIzfQ==
steps: It has mixed-case letters and digits and ends in ==, so it's probably Base64.
In CyberChef, use "From Base64". The output is FLAG{rot13_is_n0t_secur3}.
It starts with FLAG{, so you've found the flag.
blocks.answer: The flag was only Base64-encoded, which offers no protection at all.

blocks.title: Decoding relay
steps: Your teacher gives each team a sheet of ten encoded messages.
For each, identify the encoding from how it looks before decoding it.
Decode it using CyberChef (or by hand for ROT13 and binary).
The last three are layered: you'll need more than one step.

q.q: For two messages, write the encoding you spotted and the clue that told you.
q.a: E.g. "TWVzc2FnZQ== was Base64 because it had mixed-case letters and ended in ==. 4C 6F 6F 6B was hex because it was pairs of 0-9 and A-F."

q.q: Explain why Base64 shouldn't be used to protect a password.
q.a: It's encoding, not encryption: there's no secret key, so anyone can decode it instantly.

check.q: What is the main difference between encoding and encryption?
o: Encryption uses a secret key; encoding doesn't
check.why: Encoding can be reversed by anyone.

check.q: Which text is most likely Base64?
Which characters appear in hexadecimal?
What does applying ROT13 twice do?
o: Doubles the shift to 26 and scrambles it

practice.q: Explain why encoding a password in Base64 does not keep it secure.
practice.a: Base64 is encoding with no secret key (1), so anyone can decode it back to the password easily (1).

practice.q: Describe how you would recognise binary, hex and Base64.
practice.a: Binary: only 0s and 1s/groups of 8 (1); hex: digits and letters A-F, often in pairs (1); Base64: mixed-case letters/digits/+ and /, often ending in = (1).

pages.title: Hidden in plain sight
pages.spec: Explain how data can be hidden in files and images, and investigate files for hidden information
pages.summary: Steganography hides messages inside ordinary-looking files, such as in the pixels of an image. Forensic investigators also check metadata and file signatures, which can reveal what a file really is and where it came from.
pages.starter: How could you hide a secret message in a photo so nobody even knows a message exists?
sc: I can explain steganography and how it differs from encryption
I can find information in file metadata
I can use file signatures to identify a file's real type

b: Hiding a message so nobody knows it's there
Ancient version: invisible ink, messages under wax on writing tablets
Digital version: tiny changes to pixel colours that the eye can't see
Encryption hides what a message says; steganography hides that it exists
Metadata: hidden information stored with a file
Photos: date, camera, settings and sometimes GPS location
Documents: author name, edit history
Investigators (and CTF players) always check metadata
The file extension (.jpg, .pdf) is just part of the name: it can lie
A file signature ("magic number") is in the first bytes of the file
PNG files start with the bytes 89 50 4E 47 (".PNG")
Renaming a file doesn't change what it really is

blocks.text: Steganography

**[[steganography]]** means hiding a message so that nobody knows it exists. In ancient Greece, a message was reportedly tattooed on a messenger's shaved head and hidden when his hair grew back! Digital steganography hides data in ordinary files. In an image, each pixel's colour is a number; changing the last bit of each number alters the colour so slightly that no one can see it, but those bits can spell out a hidden message.

blocks.caption: Encryption vs steganography
head: Feature
Encryption
Steganography
rows: That a message exists at all
An ordinary photo, song or document

blocks.text: Metadata

**[[metadata]]** is information stored with a file, such as the date a photo was taken, the device used and sometimes GPS coordinates. Documents can store the author's name and when they were edited. **[[digital forensics]]** experts and CTF players always check metadata for clues.
Metadata can give away your location. Check your phone camera's location setting and be careful sharing original photo files.
File signatures

The extension at the end of a file name (like .jpg) can be changed by anyone. But most file types begin with a fixed pattern of bytes called a **[[file signature]]** (or "magic number"), which reveals what the file really is. For example, PNG images start with the bytes 89 50 4E 47 and PDF files start with %PDF.

blocks.title: The mystery file
blocks.context: A CTF gives you "notes.txt", but it won't open in a text editor.
steps: Open it in a hex viewer (or CyberChef) and look at the first bytes: 89 50 4E 47.
That's the PNG file signature, so it's really an image.
Rename it notes.png and open it: the image shows the flag.
blocks.answer: The extension lied; the file signature told the truth.

blocks.title: Forensics challenge
steps: Download the three challenge files from the practice CTF.
File 1: check its metadata for a hidden comment.
File 2: check its file signature and fix its extension.
File 3: use the steganography tool your teacher shows to reveal a hidden message in an image.

q.q: Which flag was hardest to find, and what technique did you use?
q.a: E.g. "The steganography one: the image looked normal, but the decoding tool revealed text hidden in the pixels' lowest bits."

q.q: Explain how a file can pretend to be a different type, and how you can tell.
q.a: The extension is just part of the name and can be changed; the file signature (first bytes of the file) shows the real file type.

check.q: What is steganography?
o: Scrambling a message with a key
Hiding a message so nobody knows it exists
check.why: It conceals existence, not just meaning.

check.q: How can a message be hidden in an image?
o: By making tiny changes to pixel colours
check.why: Changes in the lowest bits are invisible.

check.q: What is a file signature?
o: Bytes at the start of a file that show its real type

check.q: Which information might photo metadata reveal?
o: Where and when it was taken
check.why: Metadata can include GPS and time.

practice.q: Explain the difference between encryption and steganography.
practice.a: Encryption scrambles a message so it can't be read without a key (1); steganography hides the fact that a message exists at all (1).

practice.q: Explain why the file extension alone can't be trusted to tell you a file's type.
practice.a: Anyone can rename a file/change the extension (1); the file signature in its first bytes shows the real type (1).

pages.title: Web detective
pages.spec: Investigate a practice website using its source code and explain how developers protect websites
pages.summary: Everything a browser receives can be seen: HTML source, comments, scripts and cookies. CTF web challenges hide flags in these places. Real developers keep secrets on the server, validate every input and never trust what the browser sends.
pages.starter: Right-click a web page and choose "View page source". What's the strangest thing you can find?
sc: I can view a page's source and find comments and hidden elements
I can explain what cookies and robots.txt are
I can explain why secrets must never be sent to the browser

b: View source: the HTML the server sent
Developer tools (F12): inspect elements, scripts, network requests and cookies
Comments <!-- like this --> don't show on the page but are in the source
Hidden elements are only hidden from view, not from you
slides.n: Only use these tools on the practice CTF site and pages you own. Looking at public source code is normal, but trying to break into sites isn't.

b: Cookies: small pieces of data a website stores in your browser
They remember logins, settings and shopping baskets
robots.txt: a public file telling search engines what not to list
Ironically, it can point attackers to "secret" pages
Never put secrets (passwords, keys) in HTML or JavaScript
Check permissions on the server, every time
Validate all input; never trust anything from the browser
Regular testing, including paid ethical hackers

blocks.text: Your browser sees everything

When you visit a website, the **[[server]]** sends your browser the page's **[[source code]]** (HTML, CSS and JavaScript). You can see all of it: right-click and choose **View page source**, or open **[[developer tools]]** with F12. CTF web challenges hide flags in places like:

items: HTML comments, which never appear on the page: `<!-- FLAG{...} -->`
Elements hidden with CSS
JavaScript files
Cookies

blocks.text: Cookies and robots.txt

A **[[cookie]]** is a small piece of data a website stores in your browser, for example to remember that you're logged in. **robots.txt** is a public file telling search engines which pages not to list. It's meant for search engines, but it can accidentally point people to pages the owner wanted to keep quiet.

Looking at a page's source code is completely normal and legal: browsers are built to let you. Trying to access parts of a real site you're not authorised to use is not. In this lesson, only investigate the practice CTF website.
Defending websites

blocks.title: Developer rules of thumb
items: Anything sent to the browser is public: never put secrets in it
Check who the user is and what they're allowed to do on the server, for every request
Validate all input, because users (and attackers) can change anything in the browser
Don't rely on hiding things: hidden isn't secure
Pay ethical hackers to test the site, and fix what they find

blocks.title: Web detective challenges
steps: Open the practice website your teacher gives you (a CTF site built for this).
Find flags hidden in: an HTML comment, a hidden element, a JavaScript file, a cookie and the robots.txt file.
For each flag, write one rule a developer should have followed to avoid the problem.

q.q: List the flags you found and where each was hidden.
q.a: E.g. "FLAG{c0mm3nts} in an HTML comment; FLAG{cs5_h1dd3n} in a div with display:none; FLAG{c00k13} in a cookie; FLAG{r0b0ts} on a page listed in robots.txt."

q.q: For two of them, write the developer rule that would have prevented it.
q.a: E.g. "Never put secrets in HTML comments, because all source code is visible. Don't rely on robots.txt or hidden pages for security; protect pages with proper logins on the server."

check.q: How can you see a web page's HTML?
o: View page source or developer tools
check.why: Browsers let you see source code.

check.q: Why are HTML comments a bad place for secrets?
o: Anyone can read them in the source code

check.q: What is a cookie?
o: A small piece of data a website stores in your browser

check.q: What should developers do with input from the browser?
o: Validate it on the server, never trusting it

practice.q: Explain why hiding a page by not linking to it is not real security.
practice.a: Anyone who finds or guesses the address/sees it in robots.txt or source can still open it (1); real security needs server-side checks/login/permissions (1).

practice.q: Give two places in a web page where a CTF might hide a flag.
practice.a: Any two: HTML comment (1); hidden element (1); JavaScript file (1); cookie (1); robots.txt (1).

pages.title: Report it, don't exploit it
pages.spec: Describe responsible disclosure and bug bounties, and explore careers in cyber security
pages.summary: When ethical hackers find a weakness, they report it privately so it can be fixed (responsible disclosure). Many companies pay bug bounties for this. Cyber security is a growing career with many routes in, including competitions, apprenticeships and degrees.
pages.starter: You notice your school's website shows other pupils' details if you change a number in the web address. What should you do?
sc: I can explain what a bug bounty is
I can describe routes into cyber security careers

b: A vulnerability is a weakness that could be exploited
Responsible disclosure: tell the owner privately and give them time to fix it
Don't test further, don't share it, don't use it
At school: tell a teacher or the IT team straight away
slides.n: Starter answer: stop, don't look at any more records, and tell a teacher or IT immediately. Don't share the trick.

b: Companies pay rewards to people who report vulnerabilities properly
Run by big tech firms, banks and governments
Strict rules: only test what's in scope, never harm users or data
Some ethical hackers earn a living from bug bounties
Penetration tester, security analyst, incident responder, digital forensics investigator, security engineer
Belfast and Northern Ireland are home to many cyber security companies
Routes: GCSE and A level, apprenticeships, degrees, CyberFirst schemes
Start now: CTFs, CyberFirst competitions and coding clubs

blocks.text: Responsible disclosure
A **[[vulnerability]]** is a weakness that could be exploited to cause harm. When ethical hackers find one, they follow **[[responsible disclosure]]**:

items: Stop: don't explore further or access anyone's data.
Report it privately to the owner, with enough detail to fix it.
Give them time to fix it before telling anyone else.
Never use or share the weakness.

blocks.text: If you notice something wrong with a school or real-world system by accident, stop straight away and tell a teacher or the IT team. Don't "check it again" or show friends: that could become unauthorised access.
Bug bounties

A **[[bug bounty]]** is a reward paid by an organisation to people who responsibly report vulnerabilities in its systems. Big technology companies, banks and governments run bug bounty programmes with clear rules about what may be tested. Rewards range from thank-you messages to very large payments for serious problems.
Careers in cyber security

blocks.caption: Cyber security jobs
head: Job
What they do
rows: Legally attacks systems to find weaknesses
Monitors networks for attacks and responds
Contains and investigates attacks when they happen
Recovers and analyses evidence from devices

blocks.text: Demand for cyber security skills is high across the UK, and Belfast has become a major hub for cyber security companies. Routes in include GCSE and A level Digital Technology or Computer Science, degree apprenticeships, university degrees, and the NCSC's **CyberFirst** programme, which runs competitions, courses and bursaries for young people.

blocks.title: Start building skills now
items: Take part in CTFs and CyberFirst competitions
Learn programming and how networks work
Practise only on legal training platforms
Build a record of what you've learned

blocks.title: Write a disclosure report
steps: Read the scenario: while using a (fictional) cinema booking website, you notice changing the booking number in the address shows someone else's booking.
Write a short responsible disclosure email to the cinema: what you found, how they can see it, why it matters, and what you did and didn't do.
Swap with another pair and check: is it clear, polite and responsible?

q.a: A good email is polite, sent privately to the company's security contact, explains the problem clearly (changing the number in the URL shows other bookings), explains the risk (customers' names and booking details exposed), states the writer stopped immediately and didn't save or share any data, and offers to help.

q.q: Explain why you should not test the problem further or post about it online.
q.a: Further testing could access more people's data, which is unauthorised access and could harm them; posting it before it's fixed would let criminals exploit it.

check.q: What is responsible disclosure?
o: Privately reporting a vulnerability so it can be fixed
check.why: Report privately, give time to fix.

check.q: What is a bug bounty?
o: A reward for responsibly reporting a vulnerability

check.q: You accidentally see other pupils' data on a school system. What should you do?
o: Look at more records to check
Stop and tell a teacher or IT straight away

check.q: What does a penetration tester do?
o: Legally attacks systems to find weaknesses

practice.q: Describe the steps an ethical hacker should follow after finding a vulnerability.
practice.a: Stop/don't go further (1); report privately to the owner (1); give time to fix and don't share/use it (1).

practice.q: Name two jobs in cyber security and what each does.
practice.a: Any two with descriptions, e.g. penetration tester: legally tests systems (1); security analyst: monitors for attacks (1); incident responder/forensics/security engineer (1).
